Confidence Interval for Generalized Eta Squared (Approximate)

Source: R/ci_eta_squared_generalized.R
ci_eta_squared_generalized.Rd

Returns the point estimate of generalized eta squared (\(\eta^2_G\); Olejnik & Algina, 2003) along with an optional confidence interval computed by one of two approximate methods. The default is to return only the point estimate (method = "none"), because both available CI methods are approximations whose coverage properties have not been broadly validated for this estimand and warrant independent evaluation before being used in substantive inference.

Usage

ci_eta_squared_generalized(
  object = NULL,
  observed = NULL,
  SS_effect = NULL,
  SS_observed = NULL,
  SS_error = NULL,
  F_effect = NULL,
  df_effect = NULL,
  F_observed = NULL,
  df_observed = NULL,
  df_error = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  method = c("none", "parametric", "bootstrap"),
  B = 10000L,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

object

Optional. A fitted model object of class aov, lm, or aovlist (multi-stratum aov fit for within-subjects / mixed designs).

observed

Character vector of factor names treated as measured.

SS_effect, SS_observed, SS_error

Sums of squares (option 2 in eta_squared_generalized): SS_effect for the focal effect, SS_error for its error term, and SS_observed (a scalar or a vector) for every other source in the denominator of \(\eta^2_G\). The estimate depends on SS_observed and SS_error only through their sum. The parametric interval is built on the F they imply, \((\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}/df_{\text{effect}})/(\mathit{SS}_{\text{error}}/df_{\text{error}})\), which is the F of the effect's test only when SS_error is the sum of squares that test divides by: the residual, adjusted for any covariate, in a design without an Error() term, and in a design with one the residual of the stratum in which the effect is tested (subjects within groups for an effect tested between subjects, and in a one-way within-subjects design the interaction of subjects and the within-subjects factor). SS_observed then holds the other sources that Olejnik and Algina (2003, Eq. 5, p. 437) place in the denominator: the measured factors, the interactions that contain one, the covariates, and the residuals of the other strata, such as that of the subjects stratum of a within-subjects design. The interval also needs df_effect, df_error, and N.

F_effect, df_effect, F_observed, df_observed, df_error

F-values and degrees of freedom (option 3 in eta_squared_generalized). Each F divides a mean square by the focal effect's error mean square: F_effect is the effect's test, and F_observed covers the sources that SS_observed holds, so for a source in another stratum it is not the F that summary() of the fit reports. df_effect and df_error go with the sums of squares as well. Given with the sums of squares, F_effect, F_observed, and df_observed must describe the same test: the F the sums of squares imply for the effect, and the ratio of SS_observed to SS_error, must agree with the F interface's to a relative tolerance of 1e-6, the tolerance eta_squared_generalized applies to the two estimates, and the interval is then formed from the F-values. The two can agree on the estimate and still imply different F statistics for the effect, and so different intervals; such a call is refused.

N

Total sample size, with which the confidence limits for the noncentrality parameter are converted (see Details). Required when method = "parametric" and no fitted model is supplied; ignored when method = "none" or when a fitted model is supplied, in which case a single-stratum fit is converted with nobs(object) and each effect of an aovlist fit with the size of its own stratum, as in ci_eta_squared. For an effect tested in an Error() stratum, give the size of that stratum instead: the number of subjects for an effect tested between subjects, and for an effect tested within subjects the stratum's total degrees of freedom, which is df_effect + df_error when the effect is the only one tested in its stratum. N must be finite and at least df_effect + df_error.

method

One of "none" (default), "parametric", or "bootstrap". See Details.

B

Number of bootstrap replications when method = "bootstrap", a single whole number. Default 10000. The fewest accepted is 1000 through the 98 percent level (this function's own floor) and 2000 at the 99 percent level, where 10 replications beyond each limit take that many; a smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). A reported interval deserves 10000 or more. See Bootstrap replications under Details and dmar_bootstrap.

conf_level

Desired confidence coverage; default 0.95.

alpha_lower, alpha_upper

Optional Type I error on the lower and upper side. The table records the coverage, 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper, as its level and, when the two tail areas differ, the areas themselves, which the line beneath the printed table, results_sentence, and the alpha_lower and alpha_upper columns of tidy() state; with a tail area of 0 the interval is a one-sided confidence bound.

seed

Optional integer seed for the bootstrap, for reproducibility. Used locally: the caller's random number generator state is restored on exit. Default NULL draws the resamples from the current random number stream, which advances that stream.

Value

A data.frame with one row per focal effect and the columns effect, eta_squared_generalized, ci_lower, ci_upper, and method. For aovlist fits a stratum column is also present. When method = "none", the limit columns contain NA. Otherwise the table records the confidence level of its intervals in its conf_level attribute: conf_level, or 1 - alpha_lower - alpha_upper when the tail areas are supplied. With method = "bootstrap" the attributes B, B_used, n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status record the replications (see Bootstrap replications under Details).

Details

Why CI = "none" is the default. Confidence interval construction for \(\eta^2_G\) is not as settled as for partial \(\eta^2\) or \(\omega^2\), because the denominator mixes sums of squares from heterogeneous sources (the focal effect, one or more measured factors, and the error term). No noncentral F transformation maps the population noncentrality parameter directly to \(\eta^2_G\). Both methods below are approximations and are exposed for exploration rather than as defaults.

method = "parametric". The function first obtains a confidence interval for the population noncentrality parameter \(\lambda\) of the focal effect's F-test via ci_nc_F and maps its limits through the partial \(\eta^2\) transformation \(\eta^2_{p,\text{bound}} = \lambda_{\text{bound}}/(\lambda_{\text{bound}} + N)\), as ci_eta_squared converts them: N is the number of observations for a fit without an Error() term (the convention of ci_pvaf and ci_omega_squared as well), the size of the effect's stratum for an effect of an aovlist fit (see below), and N as supplied for the raw interfaces. The limits are then re-expressed as \(\eta^2_G\) bounds via $$\eta^2_{G,\text{bound}} = \frac{r_{\text{bound}}}{r_{\text{bound}} + r_{\text{obs}} + 1},$$ where \(r_{\text{bound}} = \eta^2_{p,\text{bound}}/(1-\eta^2_{p,\text{bound}}) = \lambda_{\text{bound}}/N\) and \(r_{\text{obs}}\) is the sum of the other sums of squares in the denominator of \(\eta^2_G\) (those of the measured sources and, for an aovlist fit, the residuals of the other strata) divided by the focal effect's error sum of squares. The point estimate is the same map applied to \(\mathit{SS}_{\text{effect}}/\mathit{SS}_{\text{error}} = F \cdot df_{\text{effect}}/df_{\text{error}}\), which for a fitted model converges to \(\lambda/N\) as the sample grows. When \(r_{\text{obs}}\) is 0, as in a fit without an Error() term in which nothing measured enters the denominator, \(\eta^2_G\) is the partial \(\eta^2\), and the interval is the exact one ci_eta_squared(estimand = "partial") gives. Otherwise the interval is not exact, and no conversion of the limits for \(\lambda\) can make it so: \(\eta^2_G\) then depends on the value that \(r_{\text{obs}}\) converges to as well as on \(\lambda\), while the distribution of the focal F depends on \(\lambda\) alone, so the transformation principle behind the exact intervals (Steiger, 2004, Proposition 1, p. 167), which maps the limits through a function of that one parameter, does not apply. The interval takes \(r_{\text{obs}}\) as known and equal to its sample value, which leaves the sampling variability of \(r_{\text{obs}}\) out of it. Its coverage has not been validated, and it should be treated as preliminary.

method = "bootstrap". A residual bootstrap from the fitted model: the resampling unit is a residual, drawn nonparametrically from the model's own residuals rather than from a fitted distribution. For each of the B replications, the response is regenerated as \(\hat{y}_i + \varepsilon^*_i\) where \(\varepsilon^*\) is sampled with replacement from the model's residuals; the model is refit; \(\eta^2_G\) is recomputed; and the percentile interval, the empirical quantiles of the B bootstrap values (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993), is reported. The percentile interval is the only bootstrap interval offered; there is no bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) variant. Bootstrap results vary from run to run; supply seed for reproducibility. Requires a single-stratum aov/lm fit. Not yet supported for aovlist (multi-stratum / within-subjects) fits, since the bootstrap needs to respect the subject-level correlation structure, which naive residual resampling does not. Use method = "parametric" for aovlist fits. Coverage has not been broadly validated for this estimand.

Bootstrap replications. The limits are quantiles of the B replicated values of each effect, read at alpha_lower and 1 - alpha_upper. The function requires at least 1000 replications, more than the 400 that 10 replications beyond each limit take at the 95 percent level; at the 99 percent level that count is 2000 and governs. A replication in which \(\eta^2_G\) for some effect is undefined (the refit fails, or the effect size cannot be computed from it) is dropped and counted, never replaced, and the interval is computed from the rest. The result records B (requested), B_used (the number the interval rests on), n_dropped, and B_required (the fewest replications a request may ask for; that count is held to B, not to B_used) as attributes, with bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"). One warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped states the counts when any replication was dropped, with a caution when the dropped replications are at least the 2.5 percent of B that lies beyond one limit at the 95 percent level, because they could then decide by themselves where that limit falls. When more than half were dropped, the limits of every effect are NA, the estimate is returned, and the warning has class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. With several effects, B_used is the fewest replications the limits of any effect rest on. options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) lets a smaller B (2 or more) run for a first look or a demonstration; every such call gives a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_exploratory and the result is not one to report. See dmar_bootstrap for the rule and its reasons.

Within-subjects designs (aovlist). Each focal effect's parametric interval is built from its own stratum's F test, and its limits for \(\lambda\) are converted with the size of that stratum, as ci_eta_squared converts them: the stratum's total degrees of freedom for an effect tested within subjects, and the number of subjects for an effect in the between-subjects stratum of a mixed design. \(r_{\text{obs}}\) includes the residual sums of squares of the other strata, since every source of variance that involves subjects belongs to the denominator of \(\eta^2_G\) (Olejnik & Algina, 2003, Eq. 5, p. 437; Bakeman, 2005, p. 381). With \(r_{\text{obs}}\) at the value it converges to, the conversion maps each limit for \(\lambda\) to the corresponding value of the population \(\eta^2_G\) of Olejnik and Algina (2003, Eq. 2, p. 436), the value the estimate converges to as subjects are added. In a one-way within-subjects design with n subjects, p occasions, and compound symmetry, for which Steiger (2004, Eq. 58, p. 177) gives \(\lambda = n \sum_j (\mu_j - \mu)^2 / [\sigma^2 (1 - \rho)]\), that value is \(\lambda (1 - \rho)/[\lambda (1 - \rho) + np]\): the variance of the occasion means, \(\sum_j (\mu_j - \mu)^2 / p\), over the sum of that variance and \(\sigma^2\), which holds the subject, subject by occasion, and error variances that Olejnik and Algina (2003, p. 443, note 1) place in the denominator. Given \(\lambda\), that value still depends on \(\rho\), and the distribution of the occasions' F, which depends on \(\lambda\) alone, carries no further information about \(\rho\). Steiger (2004, pp. 176–177) notes that in repeated measures designs \(\lambda\) confounds the effect with the correlation among the observations, and that the root-mean-square standardized effect of such a design cannot be estimated directly with the exact noncentral methods unless \(\rho\) is known. Converted with the number of rows, \(np\), the limits would be for a smaller quantity than the one the estimate estimates: for the three IQ occasions of pygmalion analyzed in vignette("DMAR", package = "DMAR"), 930 rows against F(2, 618) give the interval [.019, .037], below the estimate of .041; converted with 2 + 618 = 620, the interval is [.029, .054]. As eta_squared_generalized does, the function stops when an effect is tested in more than one stratum, as happens when observations are missing within subjects or a covariate varies within them, since no one stratum's sum of squares is then the effect's.

References

Algina, J., Keselman, H. J., & Penfield, R. D. (2005). An alternative to Cohen's standardized mean difference effect size: A robust parameter and confidence interval in the two independent groups case. Psychological Methods, 10(3), 317–328. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.10.3.317

Bakeman, R. (2005). Recommended effect size statistics for repeated measures designs. Behavior Research Methods, 37(3), 379–384. doi:10.3758/BF03192707

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K., & Preacher, K. J. (2012). On effect size. Psychological Methods, 17, 137–152. doi:10.1037/a0028086

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 3 on \(\eta^2\), Chapter 7 on factorial designs, and Chapter 11 on generalized \(\eta^2\) for within-subjects designs.)

Olejnik, S., & Algina, J. (2003). Generalized eta and omega squared statistics: Measures of effect size for some common research designs. Psychological Methods, 8(4), 434–447. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.4.434

Smithson, M. (2001). Correct confidence intervals for various regression effect sizes and parameters: The importance of noncentral distributions in computing intervals. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 61, 605–632. doi:10.1177/00131640121971392

Steiger, J. H. (2004). Beyond the F test: Effect size confidence intervals and tests of close fit in the analysis of variance and contrast analysis. Psychological Methods, 9(2), 164–182. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.9.2.164

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The pygmalion expectancy experiment: treatment is manipulated, while
# grade is a measured classification, so grade belongs in the denominator.
pyg <- pygmalion
pyg$grade <- factor(pyg$grade)
fit <- aov(iq_8 ~ treatment * grade, data = pyg)

# The default returns the point estimate and leaves the limits NA, because
# both interval methods are approximations.
ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade")
#> No CI computed (method = 'none'). Set method = 'parametric' for an approximate noncentral F transformation, or method = 'bootstrap' for a residual bootstrap (requires a fitted model). Both methods are approximate; see ?ci_eta_squared_generalized.
#>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method
#>  treatment       0.020                   <NA>     <NA>     none  
#>  grade           0.044                   <NA>     <NA>     none  
#>  treatment:grade 0.019                   <NA>     <NA>     none  

# The parametric approximation maps a noncentral F interval for the focal
# effect through the observed sums of squares. Warnings mark the method as
# preliminary and report that the interaction's lower limit is clamped at
# 0; treat the limits accordingly.
ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade", method = "parametric")
#> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated.
#> Warning: The observed F_value is below the alpha_lower critical value of the central F-distribution, so the lower confidence limit on generalized eta squared is 0.
#>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method    
#>  treatment       0.020                   0.001    0.058    parametric
#>  grade           0.044                   0.001    0.081    parametric
#>  treatment:grade 0.019                   0.000    0.041    parametric
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# The third option is a residual bootstrap, which refits the model once per
# replication. B = 100 keeps the example quick and is below the 1000 the
# function requires; the option lets it run and the warning says so. A
# reported interval deserves B = 10000 or more. The seed makes the
# interval reproducible and leaves the random number stream of the
# surrounding session as it was.
old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)
ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit, observed = "grade",
                           method = "bootstrap", B = 100, seed = 113)
#> Warning: Bootstrap CI resamples the fitted model's residuals nonparametrically (B = 100). Coverage has not been broadly validated for generalized eta squared; results should be treated as preliminary.
#> Warning: ci_eta_squared_generalized(): B = 100 is below the 1000 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 100 replications each limit rests on about 2.5 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 1000. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result.
#>  effect          eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method   
#>  treatment       0.020                   0.001    0.059    bootstrap
#>  grade           0.044                   0.022    0.108    bootstrap
#>  treatment:grade 0.019                   0.007    0.083    bootstrap
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 100 replications, 100 used (0 dropped; at least 1000 must be requested). Exploratory: below the number required for a reported interval.
options(old)

# The parametric treatment row from summary statistics, as an ANOVA table
# reports them: the sums of squares of treatment, of its error term (the
# residual), and of the measured sources in its denominator (grade and
# the treatment by grade interaction), with the degrees of freedom and
# the number of children for the interval.
tab <- anova(fit)
ci_eta_squared_generalized(
  SS_effect   = tab["treatment", "Sum Sq"],
  SS_observed = tab[c("grade", "treatment:grade"), "Sum Sq"],
  SS_error    = tab["Residuals", "Sum Sq"],
  df_effect   = tab["treatment", "Df"], df_error = tab["Residuals", "Df"],
  N = nobs(fit), method = "parametric")
#> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated.
#>  effect  eta_squared_generalized ci_lower ci_upper method    
#>  overall 0.020                   0.001    0.058    parametric
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# Within-subjects ANOVA. The parametric CI uses each effect's own stratum
# and converts its limits with that stratum's size.
set.seed(113)
n <- 20
rm_data <- data.frame(
  subject = factor(rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)),
  time    = factor(rep(c("Pre", "Mid", "Post"), n),
                   levels = c("Pre", "Mid", "Post")),
  y       = rnorm(n, sd = 1.5)[rep(seq_len(n), each = 3)] +
            0.7 * rep(1:3, n) + rnorm(n * 3, sd = 1.2)
)
fit_rm <- aov(y ~ time + Error(subject/time), data = rm_data)
ci_eta_squared_generalized(fit_rm, method = "parametric")
#> Warning: Parametric CI uses an approximate transformation that maps the partial eta squared CI through the observed sums of squares for measured factors. Coverage properties have not been broadly validated; results should be treated as preliminary and independently evaluated.
#>  effect eta_squared_generalized stratum      ci_lower ci_upper method    
#>  time   0.097                   subject:time 0.008    0.203    parametric
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
